name: Cumans and Kipchaks
summary: Turkic nomads who dominated the steppe from the Danube to Kazakhstan before the Mongol conquest, fighting and allying with Kyivan Rus’, Byzantium, Georgia and Hungary.

knownFor.label: Stone baba statues
knownFor.note: Stone figures placed on steppe burial mounds.

knownFor.label: Codex Cumanicus
knownFor.note: A dictionary of the Cuman language, written around 1300.

location.value: A shifting area north of the Black Sea and along the Volga, called Cumania; the confederation ran from the Danube in the west to Taraz, Kazakhstan, in the east.

terrain.value: The open grassland of the Eurasian steppe, from the Danube to Kazakhstan.

climate.value: Continental, with hot summers, cold winters and little rain.

resources.value: Pasture for horses, sheep and cattle.

urbanisation.value: Mobile camps of tents and wagons; a few winter settlements.

migration.value: Entered the southern Russian steppe in the 11th century (Bessarabia about 1068–1078). After 1241 many left for the Balkans and raided Hungary; King Béla IV settled them between the Danube and Tisza.

economicBase.value: Herding, raiding and trading with neighbouring settled states.

tradeRoutes.value: Took tribute from Crimean cities and acted as middlemen between Byzantium and the East through the port of Sudak.

wealth.value: Wealth was counted in horses and herds, plus tribute and captives.

moneyAndTax.value: The article does not mention coinage; 3,000 gold bullions were paid yearly as tribute to the Hungarian king.

inequality.value: Khans and warriors held more wealth than ordinary herders.

governmentType.value: A confederation of tribes, not one state.

keyRulers.value: Khan Köten fled to Mstislav of Galich before the Mongols and was murdered in Pest on 17 March 1241.

succession.value: Leadership passed within ruling clans, often through disputes.

institutions.value: Tribal custom and councils of chiefs.

stability.value: Loose and shifting, since khans rarely controlled all the tribes.

eliteConflict.value: Rival tribes and khans competed for pasture and tribute.

armyAndTech.value: Horse archers with composite bows, which made them valued as mercenaries.

majorWars.value: A Rus’–Cuman alliance was defeated by the Mongols at the Kalka River (1223).

territoryChange.value: The Mongol invasion of 1237–1240 ended Cuman control of the Pontic steppes in 1241.

alliancesRivals.value: David IV of Georgia married a Cuman king’s daughter (year not given); Elizabeth the Cuman was queen of Hungary 1272–77; Cuman troops fought for Rudolf of Habsburg at the Marchfeld (1278).

inventions.value: Few inventions are recorded; the Cumans are known for carved stone statues (balbals).

scienceEducation.value: Little writing; the Codex Cumanicus (1300s) is a word list made by missionaries.

openness.value: Open to trade and marriages with neighbours.

communicationTransport.value: Horses and wagons carried people and goods.

religion.value: Shamanism (Tengrism in the infobox); Christian conversions in Hungary (1089) and Georgia; Golden Horde Cumans adopted Islam in the 13th–14th centuries.

languageWriting.value: Cuman, the best-known early Turkic language, used as a lingua franca in Crimea.

artsArchitecture.value: Stone balbals placed around graves, said to represent enemies the dead had killed.

sharedIdentity.value: A shared Kipchak Turkic language and culture across the steppe.

dailyLife.value: Felt yurts at first, later light felt tents carried on wagons; herds of horses, sheep, goats, camels and cattle.

neighbours.value: Kyivan Rus’, Byzantium, Georgia, Hungary, Volga Bulgaria.

ideasReligions.value: Kipchak words and customs spread across the steppe, and many Cumans later adopted Christianity or Islam.

colonisation.value: None; they remained nomads until the Mongol conquest of 1237–41.

riseSignals.value: Moved west into the Pontic steppe in the 11th century, replacing the Pechenegs.

peakPeriod.value: The 12th century, when they raided and allied with Rus’ princes and Byzantium.

outcome.value: The Cumans who stayed joined the Golden Horde; the article does not say Kipchak was its official language.
